SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Gender identity development is a normal part
of human development. Petitioners and their
supporting amici paint a picture of transgender youth
that scientific evidence does not support. In this brief,
Amici offer the Court scientific research and clinical
experience that Petitioners leave out.
Petitioners cast the experience of raising and
supporting a transgender or gender expansive child as
a cognizable harm, but neither science nor common
sense supports the premise that there is any injury to
the parents in this case . As this brief demonstrates,
Petitioners’ claims are  belied by scientific evidence
that when transgender youth are supported at home,
they experience positive outcomes.
Nothing in Washington law prevents
Petitioners from disagreeing with the medical
consensus or from parenting their children according

3
to their convictions. Petitioners’ disagreement with
their children’s gender identity, and with the
availability of gender -affirming care generally, does
not constitute a cognizable injury in this case. The
disagreement is speculative because, as Washington
construes its laws, youth can only access a referral to
outpatient mental health services. Resp’t Br. at 12 –
14. Nor have Petitioners alleged their children have
run away or plan to run away to a licensed shelter
since Washington amended its laws . Id. at 16; Pet.
App. at 14a–15a. Petitioners’ allegations that they
have altered their parenting choices because they are
afraid their children might run away and access
medically necessary health care while at a licensed
shelter are the precise kind of speculative, self -
imposed “injur ies” the Court rejected in Clapper v.
Amnesty International USA, 568 U.S. 398, 416 (2013).
As this Court has held, Petitioners “cannot
manufacture standing merely by inflicting harm on
themselves based on their fears of hypothetical future
harm that is not certainly impending.” Ibid.
This brief demonstrates there is no causal
connection between Petitioners’ hypothetical fears
and Washington’s laws, making Petitioners’ alleged
harms neither fairly traceable to the statutes at issue
nor redressable by their challenge. There is no
evidence that the existence of Washington’s statutes
will encourage or “lure” children to run away or to
transition. Conversely, significant evidence suggests
that transgender youth have strongly held, persistent
self-knowledge about their gender. Any breakdown in
the parent -child relationship in the hypotheticals
posited by Petitioners would be the result of
Petitioners’ disapproval of their transgender child, not
Washington’s laws. No research supports Petitioners’

4
proposition that transgender youth are more likely to
run away when laws such as Washington’s are in
place; such risk is only redressable through
Petitioners’ own choices, not Washington’s statutes.
Petitioners’ standing theory rests on
assumptions about gender identity development  and
predictions about how their children would respond to
Washington's laws that science contradicts. Without
those premises, Petitioners lack Article III standing to
challenge Washington’s laws.
ARGUMENT
I. Transgender youth have a strong and
stable understanding of who they are.
Like all young people, transgender youth
typically develop a consistent, persistent, and
insistent sense of their gender identity as part of
childhood and adolescent development. Research
shows transgender and cisgender (i.e., non -
transgender) youth both develop a comparably strong

confers jurisdiction to federal courts over “cases” and
“controversies.” Standing is a “bedrock constitutional
requirement that this Court has applied to all manner
of important disputes.”  FDA v. All. for Hippocratic
Med., 602 U.S. 367, 378 (2024) (quoting United States

federal jurisdiction bears the burden of establishing
these elements.” Lujan, 504 U.S. at 561. Here,
Petitioners have neither an injury-in-fact nor a causal
connection to Washington’s laws , and  their alleged
harms are not redressable by this challenge.
A. Harms alleged by Petitioners are selfimposed and do not constitute an injuryin-fact.
The Ninth Circuit in its straightforward
application of this Court’s standing jurisprudence
properly concluded Petitioners have not demonstrated
an injury -in-fact because their alleged injuries are
“self-inflicted” and a voluntary response to
Washington’s statutes, not  a requirement the laws
impose. Int’l Partners for Ethical Care Inc . v.
Ferguson, 146 F.4th 841, 849 (9th Cir. 2025) , cert.
granted sub nom. Int’l Partners for Ethical Care, Inc.
v. Ferguson, 146 S. Ct. 2804 (2026).
Petitioners’ claims of harm include alleged
changes they made to their parenting styles around
discussions of gender, use of their children’s name s
and pronouns, and disciplinary choices, to attempt to

that might cause  their children to run away from
home. Pet. Br. at 3–4. As the Ninth Circuit panel
properly concluded, these  are independent choices
parents are free to make, none of which are the subject
or result of Washington’s laws. Washington’s laws do
not regulate parental speech and “have no bearing on
whether and to what extent Plaintiffs are permitted
to speak about topics, such as gender, with or around
